categories.name: Portfolio baseline (typical drift below recency)
categories.definition: The model's starting point before any item information: across the training data the typical item sells about 12% less in the next four months than its last-3-months run rate, so this is a portfolio-wide drift, not an item story.
categories.evidence: The SHAP base value (about -0.13 log units, nearly constant within an origin, sd 0.02). It is identical for every item in an origin, so it should never be cited as the reason one item differs from another; only mention it when the total predicted deviation is small and the base is most of it.
categories.sign_notes: Always negative (about -0.10 to -0.15). A predicted deviation close to -0.13 means 'nothing special about this item: normal decay from recency'.

categories.name: Short-term momentum (recent weeks' buzz or cooling)
categories.definition: Whether the item's sales in the last 1-4 weeks and last month are running above or below its 3-month level, i.e. a short-term fashion trend or fading buzz that recency has not yet absorbed, including reversion after a recent spike.
categories.evidence: SHAP on f_r7, f_r28, lagr1, lagr2 and peak_r. f_r7 / f_r28 are the root split of every highest-gain tree (thresholds around -0.04 to -0.17 for f_r7, about 0 for f_r28), so look first at whether f_r7 and f_r28 are below or above roughly zero. A high peak_r (recent peak well above level, split near 1.3) signals a spike that is expected to fade.
categories.sign_notes: f_r7, f_r28, lagr1 > 0 (recent weeks hotter than the 3-month level) -> positive SHAP; < 0 (cooling) -> negative SHAP, often the single largest negative term. High peak_r -> negative (spike reverts). Mean of the group is near zero overall but swings by origin month (+0.18 at Jul and Nov origins, -0.18 at Jan).

categories.name: Item life cycle (longer-run sales trajectory)
categories.definition: Where the item sits on its own multi-month trajectory - still growing, plateaued, or in long decline after its peak - as seen in the 3-6 month sales history and the 91-day slope; the item-level long-term fashion trend.
categories.evidence: SHAP on lagr3, lagr4, lagr5, lagr6 and trend91. lagr6 is the 4th most important feature overall. Large positive lagr5/lagr6 (item sold much more 5-6 months ago than now) indicates an item past its peak; negative lagr4-6 indicates a newer or growing item. Check trend91's sign for a consistent slope.
categories.sign_notes: Items that were bigger 4-6 months ago (lagr4-6 > 0) usually get negative SHAP (continued decline); items smaller back then (lagr4-6 < 0, rising) get positive SHAP. trend91 > 0 -> positive, < 0 -> negative. Caution: lagr5/lagr6 also look back half a year, so for seasonal items they can carry an opposite-season echo rather than a true life-cycle signal.

categories.name: Upcoming events and occasions
categories.definition: Demand pulled forward by US events or occasions that fall in the four target months (spring break, prom, graduation, back to school, Halloween, festivals, holiday parties, Valentine's, etc.), weighted by how well the item fits that occasion.
categories.evidence: SHAP on ev_<event>_t, x_bts, x_halloween, x_party, x_festival, occ_next and occ_n4, together with the item's occasion scores (back_to_school, party, halloween, festival). Look for a non-zero event-day count in the target window AND a high fit score for that occasion (e.g. x_bts high for a back-to-school item at a Jun-Aug origin). ev_spring_break_t is a high-gain second-level split in every top tree.
categories.sign_notes: Event in the target window and high item fit -> positive SHAP; low occ_next (occasion soon) -> positive. Event-fit items whose occasion has no days in the target window -> mildly negative. Group is strongly positive at Jun-Jul origins (+0.27, +0.13) and negative at Nov-Jan origins (-0.16 to -0.18) when combined with the hangover category.

categories.name: Event-inflated recent sales (post-event hangover)
categories.definition: Recent sales (and therefore R3) were boosted by an event in the origin window - BFCM, holidays/NYE, prom, Mother's Day, graduation, Memorial Day - so the model expects the item to fall back once the event has passed.
categories.evidence: SHAP on ev_<event>_o and occ_last. Check that the origin window actually contained the event (ev_*_o > 0, e.g. ev_bfcm_o for a Dec origin, ev_prom_o / ev_graduation_o for a Jun origin) and that occ_last is small (the item's occasion has just passed). Notable features: ev_prom_o, ev_mothers_o, ev_bfcm_o, ev_graduation_o.
categories.sign_notes: Event days in the origin window -> negative SHAP (R3 overstates normal demand); a short occ_last -> negative. Caution: ev_prom_o, ev_memorial_o and ev_graduation_o also split rows at origins where those windows are zero, so a non-zero SHAP when the event did NOT occur in the origin window is calendar information, not a hangover.

categories.name: Weather and seasonal temperature turn
categories.definition: The change in temperature between the recent window and the target months (and any unusual warmth or cold in the recent window), interacted with how warm, wintry or summery the item is: warm items rise into winter, summer items fall into autumn.
categories.evidence: SHAP on x_warm_dT, bT_dT, dT_norm, t_tgt_norm, x_winter, x_summer and the item's warmth / winter / summer / layering scores; for anomalies, ta_org, bT_ta and dT_real_from_org. Check the direction of dT_norm (target colder or warmer than origin) against the item's warmth/winter/summer scores - the signs must be consistent (e.g. high winter score and falling temperatures -> positive). x_winter, x_warm_dT and winter are high-gain splits in the top trees.
categories.sign_notes: Warm/winter item and target colder than origin (dT_norm < 0) -> positive; summer item and target colder -> negative; the reverse in spring. An unusually warm origin (ta_org > 0) for a warm item -> R3 understated -> positive, and vice versa. Group mean is about +0.13/+0.14 at Sep-Oct origins and -0.07/-0.13 at Jan-Feb origins. The anomaly features are individually weak (none in the top 40), so a story resting only on them is fragile.

categories.name: Geographic / regional climate mix
categories.definition: Where in the US the item sells: items bought mostly in warm southern states or cold northern states respond differently to the same calendar, captured through the temperature the item's customers experience and its temperature preference across states.
categories.evidence: SHAP on t_org (temperature felt by the item's regional customer mix) and beta_T (how sales shift with state temperature). Within one origin month, differences in t_org between items are purely geographic. Look for an item whose t_org is clearly above or below peers at the same origin, or a large |beta_T|. t_org is a second-level split (near 11 C) in a top Oct tree.
categories.sign_notes: Items selling in colder regions (low t_org) heading into winter tend to get positive SHAP if they are warm items and negative if they are summer items; beta_T > 0 (sells where it is hot) is negative going into cold months and positive going into warm months. This is the only geographic signal in the model: there are no explicit region features, so 'geographic trend' explanations beyond climate are not supported.

categories.name: Last year's seasonal pattern (like-for-like history)
categories.definition: How the item itself, its product type, its macro group and its occasion group moved last year over the same four months relative to the months before, plus the calendar month of the target window.
categories.evidence: SHAP on own_sea4, lfl_type4, lfl_macro4, lfl_occ4 and tmonth. Check the ratio values: own_sea4 / lfl_*4 above 1 (or above 0 on a log scale) means last year ramped up into these months. own_sea4 needs a full year of history; for young items it is missing and the type/macro ratios carry the signal.
categories.sign_notes: Last-year ramp-up into the target months -> positive; last-year drop -> negative. Group mean is mildly positive at Jun-Aug origins (+0.01/+0.02) and clearly negative at Nov-Feb origins (down to -0.10 at Dec), i.e. the post-holiday slump.

categories.name: Shopper-cluster seasonality (co-purchase neighbours)
categories.definition: What happened last year to the products that the same customers buy together with this item: if its co-purchase neighbours ramped up (or slumped) into these months, the item's customer segment is expected to do the same, and the neighbours' sales level indicates how big that segment is.
categories.evidence: SHAP on cp_nb_sea4 (the single most important feature, mean |SHAP| 0.09) and cp_nb_lvl. cp_nb_sea4 splits near 0.30-0.40 in the 2025-10 and 2026-02 top trees. Look at whether cp_nb_sea4 is high (neighbours ramped up) or low, and whether the item's own history agrees (own_sea4). Especially informative for young items without their own last-year history.
categories.sign_notes: High cp_nb_sea4 -> positive; low -> negative. On average negative in every origin month (mean -0.07), most negative at Nov-Jan origins (-0.10 to -0.13). High cp_nb_lvl (item bought alongside best-sellers) usually supports the item; low cp_nb_lvl is mildly negative.

categories.name: Product type and style profile (structural fashion trend)
categories.definition: What kind of product it is - type, fabric, sleeve, length, silhouette, print, occasion tier, and LLM-scored traits such as staple vs statement, formality, fit and versatility - capturing which categories and styles systematically outgrow or lag their recent run rate (the long-term, category-level fashion trend).
categories.evidence: SHAP on ptype (6th most important feature), the a_* tagger attributes and the descriptor scores staple, statement, versatility, formality, fit_tightness, coverage. These are static per item, so their SHAP should be read as 'items of this type/style tend to over- or under-perform recency'. Compare with other items of the same ptype at the same origin.
categories.sign_notes: Group mean is near zero but drifts with season: slightly positive at Jun-Oct origins, slightly negative at Nov-Feb. Staple / versatile items tend toward small positive or stabilising contributions; statement pieces toward larger swings and faster fade. Combined share is small (product 5.9%, descriptors 3.9%, R^2 alone 0.03 and 0.07), so it is rarely the main explanation.

categories.name: Item age and sales scale
categories.definition: Corrections for how big and how established the item is: young items whose recent level understates their run rate (partial months, still ramping) are lifted, and very high- or low-volume items are nudged toward typical behaviour.
categories.evidence: The 'level offset (young items)' term and SHAP on lvl (log recent level). The level offset is large only for items with under about 3 months of history; check the item's age / launch date. lvl has a 5% share but R^2 alone of 0.003, so treat its SHAP as a correction that interacts with other features rather than a stand-alone reason.
categories.sign_notes: Level offset is positive on average (+0.06, up to +0.10 at Feb origins) with sd 0.18: strongly positive for items launched recently, near zero for mature items. lvl SHAP is small and can go either way; very low-volume items are noisier in log terms.

categories.name: unexplained: viral, social-media or influencer spike
categories.definition: The item sold far more than the model expected because of an external attention shock (TikTok/Instagram virality, influencer post, celebrity sighting, press) that no feature in the data could see coming.
categories.evidence: Actual deviation well above the model (residual > about +0.6, i.e. more than one residual sd) with no supporting momentum at the origin (f_r7, f_r28, lagr1 near or below zero) and no event or weather story. Often a statement / trend-led item; the spike shows up abruptly in one target month rather than as a gradual seasonal ramp. Check social or marketing logs for the item.
categories.sign_notes: Positive residual (actual > model). The mirror case - the item was itself viral during the origin window and collapses afterwards - shows as a negative residual with high peak_r and f_r7 that the model only partly corrected.

categories.name: unexplained: stock-out or supply limits
categories.definition: Inventory, not demand, set the sales: the item sold out or had broken sizes in the target months (actual below model), or was out of stock during the origin window so R3 understates demand and a restock produces an apparent surge (actual above model).
categories.evidence: Negative residual for an item the model was bullish on (positive momentum, positive season/event SHAP) whose target-month sales drop abruptly or go to near zero; or a positive residual where the origin months show a sudden gap or dip (lagr1/lagr2 sharply negative, low f_r7) without a seasonal reason. Confirm with inventory, size availability or restock dates.
categories.sign_notes: Usually negative residual (sold out in target); positive residual when the origin window was depressed by a stock-out. Most likely for best-sellers and for items with strong positive model predictions.

categories.name: unexplained: promotion, markdown or clearance not in the data
categories.definition: A brand-specific price action - site-wide sale, item markdown, clearance, bundle or email/feature placement - shifted sales in either window, which the model cannot see because it has no price or marketing features beyond the generic US event calendar.
categories.evidence: Positive residual concentrated in a single target month that coincides with a known sale or end-of-season clearance (often late in a season for items with negative weather/seasonality SHAP), or a negative residual when the origin window included an item-specific promotion that inflated R3 and the generic hangover features (ev_bfcm_o etc.) did not fully cover it. Check price history and campaign calendars.
categories.sign_notes: Positive residual when the promotion falls in the target months; negative when it fell in the origin window. Clearance of out-of-season items gives positive residuals despite negative seasonal SHAP.

categories.name: unexplained: launch, sell-through or assortment decision
categories.definition: The item's trajectory was set by a merchandising decision or a launch dynamic the history does not reveal: a new item ramping faster or slower than typical, a deliberate end-of-life sell-through or delisting, a relaunch or colourway addition.
categories.evidence: Large residual for a young item where the level offset and short history dominate the SHAP (the model is guessing), or a strong negative residual where target sales fall to near zero for an otherwise healthy item (delisted or sold through). Check launch date, discontinuation flags and whether sibling variants were added or removed.
categories.sign_notes: Either sign. Young items: positive residual if the launch took off, negative if it stalled. Mature items: negative residual for discontinuation / planned sell-through; positive for relaunch or a new colourway feeding the same item ID.

categories.name: unexplained: data artefact or small-number noise
categories.definition: The deviation reflects how the data were recorded rather than real demand: very small unit counts where the +1 offset and Poisson noise dominate the log ratio, returns or cancellations netted into a month, SKU/ID remapping, or a partial month at the edge of the data.
categories.evidence: Large |residual| on items with very low lvl (a handful of units per month), erratic lagr1-lagr6 with no pattern, zero months in the middle of a selling history, or a sudden step in sales that coincides with a catalogue or ID change. Check raw order lines for the item.
categories.sign_notes: Either sign, typically large in log terms but small in units. Low-volume items dominate; such cases should carry little weight in business conclusions.

observations: Short-term momentum is the model's first question: f_r7 or f_r28 is the root split of all nine highest-gain trees at the 2025-06, 2025-10 and 2026-02 origins (gains 90-250, the largest in each tree), and recent momentum carries 27% of |SHAP| with the best stand-alone R^2 (0.33). Its sign swings with the calendar (+0.18 at Jul and Nov origins, -0.18 at Jan), so part of what looks like item-specific buzz is seasonal carry-over.

Calendar categories dominate by origin month: events/occasions are strongly positive for Jun-Jul origins (+0.27, +0.13: spring-break, summer and back-to-school windows) and strongly negative for Nov-Jan (-0.16 to -0.18, post-holiday); weather lifts Sep-Oct origins (+0.13, +0.14) and drags Jan-Feb (-0.07, -0.13); co-purchase seasonality is negative in every month and deepest Nov-Jan (-0.10 to -0.13); like-for-like seasonality reaches -0.10 in Dec. At winter origins four seasonal categories all push down together.

Those seasonal categories overlap heavily: events, temperature, co-purchase seasonality and history seasonality each explain 0.17-0.27 of the deviation alone, and x_winter / x_summer are built from event windows but behave like season-fit terms. How a seasonal effect is split between 'weather', 'event' and 'seasonal history' for one item is therefore fragile; when they agree in sign they should be read as one seasonal story.

Several 'event' splits in the top trees are really calendar indicators: ev_spring_break_t (>0 vs 0), ev_prom_o <= 40, ev_memorial_o and ev_graduation_o appear as high-gain splits even at the Oct and Feb origins where those windows are empty, partitioning training rows by time of year. Event SHAP that is non-zero when the event is not in the relevant window should not be narrated as an event effect.

cp_nb_sea4 (shopper-cluster seasonality) is the single most important feature (mean |SHAP| 0.092) and appears as a second-level split in the Oct and Feb trees, while the item's own last-year ratio own_sea4 is far weaker (0.020): the model trusts what similar customers' baskets did last year more than the item's own history. Geography enters only through climate (t_org, beta_T); the temperature-anomaly features (ta_org, bT_ta, dT_real_from_org) are not in the top 40, so 'unusual weather' explanations are weakly supported.

The model is compressed and leaves a large residual: model deviation sd 0.62 vs actual 0.88, correlation 0.78, residual sd 0.56, sign agreement 0.83 (better for top-100 items: corr 0.86). The base (-0.13, nearly constant) and the young-item level offset (+0.06 mean, sd 0.18) together are about a quarter of |SHAP| but are not item-specific stories; lvl has a 5% share yet R^2 alone 0.003, and product type plus LLM descriptors are small (9.8% combined, R^2 0.03 / 0.07), so long-term style-trend explanations are thin and big misses belong to the unexplained categories.
